summary:
Vologda Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care applies in full and no regional deviation material enough to score separately has been identified. A trans visitor therefore faces the same exposure as elsewhere in the country.

Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, so any identity check by police, at a hotel or on transport reads as a mismatch between presentation and paperwork, with no lawful route to correct it. The mismatch persists for the whole stay and cannot be resolved by carrying a foreign document.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute covers public expression, and foreign nationals who breach it face arrest, detention and deportation.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Displaying associated symbols is prosecuted separately under Article 20.3 of the administrative code.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The practical effect for a visitor is that no aspect of legal or medical gender recognition is available in-country, and any attempt to obtain it is itself an offence.

The US State Department's travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings expressly directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the same legal picture and is the standard used to assess UK asylum claims from Russia.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has risen in volume as well as severity. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation regime, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment. A further 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two preceding years. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Deaths in custody and coerced conversion practice sit alongside the court figures. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or by its repetition, may amount to persecution. It assesses the state as able but not willing to provide protection, which is the standard applied to protection claims.

The same Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. Residents face the same two-to-six-year participation penalty and six-to-ten-year organising penalty as visitors, with the additional exposure of having no route to emigrate through legal gender recognition.

Residents are liable for the propaganda provisions on the same terms as foreign nationals, including administrative fines up to 400,000 rubles and, on repetition, criminal prosecution with up to four years' imprisonment. Same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised, so the resident risk attaches to expression, symbols, organisation and documentation rather than to conduct in private.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Vologda-specific enforcement records appear in the source inventory; the oblast is assessed on the national framework because no regional deviation was identified, not because oblast-level policing has been independently verified as identical.

The regional distribution of the 101 extremism-related convictions is not broken down in the sources, so whether any occurred in Vologda Oblast is unresolved.

The sources do not disaggregate how many of the 139 people recorded as impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 were transgender rather than lesbian, gay or bisexual, so the trans-specific share of that figure is unresolved.

Whether local police, hotel staff or transport authorities in the oblast apply identity checks more or less frequently than the national average is not sourced and remains an open question.
